sections.heading: José Ángel Buesa
sections.note: The whole of *Poema del olvido*, in three parts, each read against a painting by Winslow Homer.

sections.heading: Single Lines
sections.note: Authors I copied out once and never returned to, in the order I found them.

sections.heading: Aphorisms
sections.note: They are not quotations of anyone: they are the short forms a language keeps because they say in three words something it would otherwise take a paragraph to say. Under each one is what I went and found out about it.

1603147630556635141.cite: Epílogo de El hacedor, Jorge Luis Borges
1603147630556635141.body: "Un hombre se propone la tarea de dibujar el mundo. A lo largo de los años puebla un espacio con imágenes de provincias, de reinos, de montañas, de bahías, de naves, de islas, de peces, de habitaciones, de instrumentos, de astros, de caballos y de personas. Poco antes de morir, descubre que ese paciente laberinto de líneas traza la imagen de su cara."

1606560083730735104.body: "Estas pláticas que yo tengo con mi conciencia son a veces muy largas, duran días enteros; por eso no resulta que me ponga a contártelas en esta pobre carta. De verdad, cuídate mucho, come y duerme bien y sueña con los angelitos y no en esta cosa maligna que soy yo. Pero no me olvides."

1610199841736368132.note: Japanese, 物の哀れ — “the pathos of things”. Not sadness at things but the ache of noticing that they pass: the cherry blossom is moving *because* it falls. Named by the scholar Motoori Norinaga in the eighteenth century, reading the Genji.

1610201048643428352.note: Latin, “remember that you must die”. Roman, and later carried into Christian painting as the skull set beside the books: not a threat, a measure. Whatever you are weighing, weigh it against this.

1610202456398467072.note: Latin, “time flees”. From Virgil's Georgics, where the full line is *fugit irreparabile tempus* — it flees, and it cannot be recovered. The second half is the one that bites.

1610202769020837890.note: Latin, “seize the day”. Horace, Odes I.11, and the rest of the line is usually dropped: *carpe diem, quam minimum credula postero* — seize the day, trusting tomorrow as little as you can. *Carpere* is what you do to fruit, not to a prize.

1610207756392210432.note: Latin, “art is long, life is short”. Hippocrates wrote it first in Greek and meant it of medicine: the craft takes longer to learn than a lifetime gives you. The common reading, that art outlives the artist, reverses which of the two is the problem.

1610208578186661890.note: Latin, “the golden mean”. Horace again, Odes II.10: the one who loves it keeps clear both of a hovel and of a palace worth envying. It argues for the middle not as timidity but as the only place that is not exposed.

1610211846312820739.note: Latin, “by teaching, we learn”. From a letter of Seneca: *homines dum docent discunt* — while they teach, people learn. Anyone who has had to explain something they thought they knew has met this one.

1610214149862170626.note: Latin, “dare to know”. Horace, taken up by Kant in 1784 as the motto of the Enlightenment, where he glossed it: have the courage to use your own understanding. The dare is the point; the knowing was never the hard part.

1610215075515883524.note: Latin, “if you want peace, prepare for war”. Adapted from Vegetius, a late Roman writer on military matters. It has been used ever since to justify both restraint and armament, which is a fair measure of how much it actually settles.

1610215895808221185.note: Latin, “the truth shall set you free”. John 8:32, in the Vulgate. It is carved over the entrances of a great many universities, usually without the clause before it, which makes the freedom conditional on staying in the word.

1673857183329529859.alt: A sheet of paper taped to a tiled wall with EXCELSIOR written across it by hand
1673857183329529859.alt2: Pat in close-up, looking straight down the lens, in the scene the film opens with
1673857183329529859.note: From *Silver Linings Playbook*, where Pat writes the word on a sheet of paper and tapes it to the wall. *Excelsior* is Latin for *ever upward*, and in the film it is the rule he gives himself: to keep looking for the silver lining in whatever happens. Pat Sr.’s speech from the same film is in [Cinema](/spaces/cinema/#favorite-drama-film).

garcia-marquez-cien-anos-petra-cotes.body: "Aureliano Segundo pensaba sin decirlo que el mal no estaba en el mundo, sino en algún lugar recóndito del misterioso corazón de Petra Cotes, donde algo había ocurrido durante el diluvio que volvió estériles a los animales y escurridizo el dinero. Intrigado con ese enigma, escarbó tan profundamente en los sentimientos de ella, que buscando el interés encontró el amor porque tratando de que ella lo quisiera terminó por quererla. Petra Cotes, por su parte, lo iba queriendo más a medida que sentía aumentar su cariño, y fue así como en la plenitud del otoño volvió a creer en la superstición juvenil de que la pobreza era una servidumbre del amor"
garcia-marquez-cien-anos-petra-cotes.cite: Cien años de soledad, Gabriel García Márquez
